planting.note: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed once soil has warmed well past the last frost date, into loose, sandy ground; Florunner needs the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to fill out its heavy pod load.

directions: Plant shelled seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, since the flowering pegs must push easily into the ground to form pods. Florunner was released in 1969 by the Florida Agricultural Experiment Station as a Spanish x Virginia-derived runner-type, and its spreading, decumbent habit and exceptionally heavy pod set drove a major jump in peanut yields across the Southeast when it was introduced. The sprawling vines cover more ground than bunch-type peanuts, so give plants extra room, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pegging to maximize pod set. Dig the whole plant once leaves begin to yellow in fall and cure pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling, boiling, or roasting.
sources: Crop Science Society of America registration records

planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed in loose, sandy soil once the ground has warmed well past the last frost; this variety wants a full warm season of 135 days or more to finish its pods, which the extended Gulf Coast summer readily provides.

directions: Sow shelled, unroasted seed 1.5 inches deep in loose, well-drained, sandy soil, hilling lightly around the base once yellow blooms open so the pegs that carry developing pods have an easy path into the ground. Georgia-06G was released in 2006 by the University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton and quickly became the dominant runner-type peanut grown across the Southeast, prized for strong resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus along with consistently high yield and grade quality. The dark green, decumbent runner vines spread widely, so space plants generously, and keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pegging since drought at that stage sharply reduces pod set. Dig when foliage starts to yellow and the inner pod veining has darkened, then cure the pulled plants in a warm, airy spot for a couple of weeks before shelling.

planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once it has warmed well past the last frost date; this variety is the strongest choice for Gulf Coast gardens on sandy, root-knot-nematode-prone ground where other peanuts struggle.

directions: Plant shelled, raw seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mounding soil gently at the base as flowering begins to give the pegs an easy route downward. Tifguard was released in 2007 by the USDA Agricultural Research Service and the University of Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station, bred from a cross of the nematode-resistant line 'C-99R' with the spotted-wilt-resistant 'COAN', making it the first peanut cultivar combining strong resistance to both peanut root-knot nematode and tomato spotted wilt virus. That dual resistance is especially valuable on the light, sandy Gulf Coast soils where root-knot nematode pressure often limits other peanut varieties. Keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the whole plant once foliage yellows and cure pods in a warm, airy location before shelling.
sources: University of Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station

planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once the ground is reliably warm after the last frost; the long Gulf Coast summer suits this Virginia-type peanut, which needs a full season to finish its large, two-kernel pods.

directions: Sow shelled, unroasted seed 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, hilling soil gently at the base once flowering starts so the pegs can push into the ground easily. Bailey was released in 2008 by the North Carolina State University peanut breeding program and carries partial resistance to several diseases that thrive in warm, humid Southern growing seasons, including early leaf spot, Cylindrocladium black rot, Sclerotinia blight, and tomato spotted wilt virus. As a Virginia-type peanut it produces the large, two-seeded pods favored for in-shell roasting and the classic Southern tradition of boiled peanuts, rather than the smaller kernels typical of Spanish or Valencia types. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the plant once the foliage yellows and cure the pulled pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling or boiling.

planting.note: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once it has warmed well past the last frost; give this Virginia-type peanut the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to finish its large pods.

directions: Plant shelled, raw seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mounding soil lightly around the base at flowering to give the pegs an easy path into the ground. Sugg was released in 2009 by North Carolina State University's multi-disease-resistance breeding program and stacks resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus, Cylindrocladium black rot, Sclerotinia blight, and early leaf spot into one Virginia-type line, a combination useful under the hot, humid disease pressure typical of Southern growing seasons. It carries a distinctive pink seed coat and produces a high share of the large fancy and jumbo pods valued for in-shell roasting and boiling. Keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the whole plant once foliage yellows and cure pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling.
sources: North Carolina Crop Improvement Association — Peanut Variety Information
